why: Nobody on the chain owns `fly`. The chain ends at `null`, so the answer is `undefined`. A typo like `user.nmae` is quiet in the same way.

q: If `bark` is on `Dog.prototype`, then `rex` and `fido` each carry their own copy of `bark`.
why: No. They share one function, so `rex.bark === fido.bark` is `true`. Each dog keeps only its own data, like `name`, and one hidden link. Put data on each object and functions on the prototype.

why: `in` walks up the chain, so it finds the inherited `toString`. `Object.hasOwn` looks only at the object itself, so it is `false` for `toString` and `true` for `name`.

q: Which of these does the array `[1, 2]` own itself? Use `Object.hasOwn`.
why: An array owns only its items and `length`. `map` lives once on `Array.prototype`, shared by every array. `toString` is found further up.

q: Why is `Array.prototype.last = function () { ... }` a bad idea?
options: Every array in the program and in every library shares it, and a library or a later version of JavaScript may add a different `last`
It throws an error as soon as it runs
It works only on the first array you make
why: A change to a built-in prototype reaches code you did not write. Write a normal function instead: `const last = (arr) => arr[arr.length - 1];`.

why: `a.tags` is a read, so it walks up and finds the shared array on `base`. `push` then changes that one array, and `b` sees it too. Put data on each object, not on the prototype.
